title: Meet the player
description: Let someone else name the hero.

tasks.title: Ask the player a question
tasks.body: input("What is your name? ") displays a prompt and returns the text the player types. Store that returned text in a variable so your story can use it.
tasks.detail: Here, player = input(...) saves the response. A plus sign joins strings: "Welcome, " + player. In this academy, fill in Player replies before running; Python reads those replies in order.

tasks.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome, " + player + "!")
tasks.note: With Nova as the player reply, the welcome includes Nova. Try a different reply and the story changes.

tasks.question: If the player replies Kai, what will the example display?
tasks.why: input() returns Kai. The variable player remembers that text, and print() joins it to the greeting.

tasks.prompt: Change the welcome message. Run once with Nova as the reply, then change the reply to Kai and run again.
Ask for the player’s name with input(), store the reply, and print a greeting that includes that reply. It should work for different names without editing the code.
tasks.starter:
player = input("What is your name? ")
# Print a welcome that uses player
hints: input() gives back whatever the player typed. The starter already keeps it in the variable player.
Look at the comment line: replace it with a print() that joins a greeting and player.
With other names: print("Good morning, " + friend) greets whatever is stored in friend. An f-string works too: f"See you soon, {friend}".

error_hints.text: The reply is stored in player. Check that the name inside your print() is spelled exactly the same.
A name typed straight into the greeting stays the same for every player. Use the variable player in the greeting instead.

similar_example.note: A variable inside a greeting. In your challenge, the value comes from input() instead of being typed into the code.

other_ways.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Welcome, {player}!")
other_ways.note: An f-string puts the reply straight into the greeting.

other_ways.code:
player = input("What is your name? ")
print("Welcome,", player)
other_ways.note: print() with a comma adds the space for you.

messages.message: Use the value returned by input() in your greeting. Test a different player name; a hard-coded name will not change with the reply.
Your greeting used the reply: it changed when we tried two different player names. Run it with your own name as the reply: does the greeting read the way you want?
